ai.literal: From whatever, from whatever he has separated, suffering from that, from that he is without.
ai.translation: From whatever things a person frees himself, from those very things he experiences no suffering.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் எந்தெந்தப் பொருள்களின் மீதுள்ள பற்றிலிருந்து விலகுகிறானோ, அந்தந்தப் பொருள்களால் அவனுக்குத் துன்பம் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the direct relationship between renunciation and freedom from suffering. The repeated phrase 'யாதனின் யாதனின்' (from whatever, from whatever) emphasizes that the rule applies to absolutely anything a person might be attached to. 'நீங்கியான்' refers to one who has separated himself from such attachments. By letting go of a specific thing, a person ensures that they will not experience 'நோதல்' (suffering) caused by that very thing ('அதனின் அதனின்').

ai.literal: If desired to be, let one renounce; after having renounced, here the natural things are many.
ai.translation: If you desire the highest good, renounce completely. After you have renounced, the natural benefits that accrue even here are many.
ai.modern: உண்மையான நன்மையை அடைய விரும்பினால், பற்றுக்களை முழுமையாகத் துறக்க வேண்டும். அவ்வாறு துறந்த பின், இவ்வுலகிலேயே இயல்பாகக் கிடைக்கும் நன்மைகள் பலவாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the immediate and abundant benefits of true renunciation. The phrase 'வேண்டின் உண்டாக' suggests that if one truly desires the ultimate good, they must renounce completely and effectively. 'துறந்த பின்' indicates the liberated state after letting go of worldly attachments. The words 'ஈண்டு இயற்பால பல' assure the seeker that even in this present life, the natural rewards of such detachment, like profound peace and clarity, are plentiful.

ai.literal: Destroying is necessary the five's sense-domain; leaving is necessary desired all together.
ai.translation: One must conquer the domain of the five senses. To do so, one must give up all desired things altogether.
ai.modern: ஐம்புலன்களின் ஆசைகளை அழிக்க வேண்டும்; அதற்கு நாம் விரும்பிய பொருட்கள் அனைத்தையும் ஒருசேர விட்டுவிட வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the fundamental requirement of renunciation. To achieve true detachment, one must conquer the domain of the five senses, which constantly pull the mind toward worldly objects. To succeed in this, it is necessary to completely and simultaneously give up all things one desires. The word 'ஒருங்கு' (altogether) stresses that partial renunciation is insufficient; all attachments must be abandoned at once.

ai.literal: Nature is for asceticism one-thing not-having; possession delusion becomes again having-brought-back.
ai.translation: The true nature of asceticism is to possess absolutely nothing. Owning anything will bring back delusion once again.
ai.modern: ஒரு பொருளும் இல்லாமல் இருப்பதே துறவுக்கு இயல்பாகும். ஒரு பொருளை உடைமையாகக் கொண்டாலும் அது மீண்டும் மயக்கத்தைக் கொண்டுவரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the core requirement of renunciation ('நோன்பு') as the complete absence of possessions ('ஒன்று இன்மை'). It contrasts this state of having nothing with ownership ('உடைமை'). The word 'மயல்' refers to the delusion or confusion of worldly attachments. The text warns that retaining even a single possession will bring back ('பெயர்த்து') this delusion once again ('மற்றும்'), thereby undoing the ascetic's progress.

ai.literal: Other attachment what indeed, birth severing to those who have undertaken, even the body is excess.
ai.translation: To those who have undertaken the severing of births, even their own body is a burden. What then is the purpose of other attachments?
ai.modern: பிறப்பை அறுக்க முயல்பவர்களுக்குத் தம் உடம்பே ஒரு சுமையாகும். அப்படியிருக்க, அவர்களுக்கு வேறு பற்றுதல்களால் என்ன பயன்?
ai.explanation: This couplet questions the logic of holding onto worldly attachments when the ultimate goal is renunciation. For those who have committed to ending the cycle of birth, even their own physical body is considered an excess. The word 'mikai' can mean excess, fault, or burden, and here it best means an unnecessary excess or burden. If the body itself is more than what is necessary, any other external connection or possession is entirely pointless.

ai.literal: "I" [and] "mine" which says pride he who severs, celestials-to higher world will enter.
ai.translation: He who severs the pride that says "I" and "mine" will enter a world higher than that of the celestials.
ai.modern: 'நான்', 'என்னுடையது' என்று சொல்லும் அகந்தையை வேரறுப்பவன், தேவர்களுக்கும் மேலான உயர்ந்த உலகத்தை அடைவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet identifies the core of true renunciation as the elimination of ego and possessiveness. The words 'யான்' (I) and 'எனது' (mine) represent the root causes of worldly attachment. 'செருக்கு' denotes the arrogant delusion that arises from clinging to these two concepts. By completely severing ('அறுப்பான்') this pride, a person achieves a spiritual state or realm ('உலகம்') that surpasses even the heavens of the celestial beings ('வானோர்க்கு உயர்ந்த').

words.gloss: to those who do not let go

ai.literal: Grasping and not letting go are sorrows, attachment grasping and to those who do not let go.
ai.translation: Sorrows will take hold and never let go of those who hold on to their attachments and never let them go.
ai.modern: பற்றுகளைப் பிடித்துக்கொண்டு அவற்றை விடாதவர்களை, துன்பங்களும் விடாமல் பிடித்துக்கொள்ளும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet creates a striking parallel between human action and the reaction of sorrow. The word 'பற்று' is used both as a noun meaning 'attachment' and as a verb meaning 'to grasp'. If a person grasps their attachments and refuses to let them go, sorrows will in turn grasp that person and refuse to let go. The repetition of the phrase 'பற்றி விடாஅ' (grasping and not letting go) emphasizes that suffering is the direct and inescapable mirror of clinging to worldly things.

ai.literal: Reached the highest state, completely renounced (they); having been deluded, fell into a net, other they.
ai.translation: Those who have completely renounced have reached the highest state. The others, being deluded, are caught in a net.
ai.modern: முற்றிலுமாகப் பற்றுக்களைத் துறந்தவர்கள் உயர்ந்த நிலையை அடைந்தவர்கள் ஆவர். அவ்வாறு துறக்காத மற்றவர்கள் மயக்கமடைந்து வலையில் அகப்பட்டவர்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts those who have fully renounced attachments with those who have not. The phrase 'தீரத் துறந்தார்' refers to those who have completely given up desires, and they are said to have 'தலைப்பட்டார்', meaning they have reached the highest state. The word 'தலை' (head) is used here in the sense of 'highest' or 'ultimate', which best fits the goal of renunciation. On the other hand, 'மற்றையவர்' (the others) are 'மயங்கி' (deluded by worldly illusions) and thus 'வலைப்பட்டார்', trapped in the net of worldly suffering.

ai.literal: Attachment severed at-the-very-moment birth will-cut-off; otherwise impermanence to-see will-be.
ai.translation: The very moment attachments are severed, the cycle of birth is cut off. Otherwise, one will only experience impermanence.
ai.modern: பற்று நீங்கிய அப்பொழுதே பிறவித் துன்பம் அறுபடும்; இல்லையென்றால் நிலையற்ற தன்மையே காணப்படும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the direct result of true renunciation. The word 'பற்று' refers to worldly attachments or desires. When these attachments are completely severed ('அற்ற கண்ணே'), the cycle of birth ('பிறப்பு') is immediately cut off ('அறுக்கும்'). The word 'மற்று' means 'otherwise'—if attachments remain, one will only continue to experience the impermanence ('நிலையாமை') of worldly life. The emphatic 'ஏ' in 'கண்ணே' stresses that liberation happens at the exact moment of letting go.

ai.literal: Hold on to the hold of him who is free from attachment; that hold, hold on to, in order to let go of attachment.
ai.translation: Cling to the hold of the one who has no attachments. Cling to that hold in order to let go of your own attachments.
ai.modern: எந்தப் பற்றும் இல்லாதவனுடைய பற்றினைப் பற்றிக் கொள்ளுங்கள். உங்களுடைய மற்ற பற்றுகளை விடுவதற்காகவே அந்தப் பற்றினைப் பற்றிக் கொள்ளுங்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet plays brilliantly on the word 'paṟṟu', which means both the physical act of holding on and the psychological state of attachment. It advises the seeker of renunciation to attach themselves to the one who is completely free of attachments. By holding firmly to this single, pure connection, all other worldly ties and desires can be successfully severed. The paradox of using an attachment to destroy attachments highlights the practical method of achieving true detachment.
